title: Minneapolis Institute of Art: Masterpieces
subtitle: Twenty works in which a stain, a brushstroke or a slight change of colour carries the argument.
introduction:
The blood on Lucretia's pale clothing changes how everything else in Rembrandt's painting is read. Van Gogh's olive grove makes a different demand: ground, trees and sky are distinct, yet related kinds of strokes keep movement running through them all. At the other end of this selection, Ad Reinhardt asks for attention to differences close enough to black that a quick glance may miss them.

These are three very different uses of a painted surface. This guide follows them through portraits, landscapes and a theatrical scroll at the Minneapolis Institute of Art. Sometimes paint clarifies an object; sometimes it complicates recognition. The useful question is not whether a picture looks realistic, but which distinctions its handling makes possible.
visitNote: This focused selection comes from Mia’s much wider collections. Check current object records for gallery locations, loans and rotations, particularly for works on paper. The Saint Anthony Falls painting records an earlier view, as its title makes explicit; it is not a picture of the site today.

books.title: The Practice and Science of Drawing
books.author: Harold Speed
books.note: Speed’s practical account of tone and composition can be tested against the portraits and landscapes here. Start with the dark Mancini self-portrait and the pale forms of Poussin, where very different distributions of light guide recognition.

works.title: Olive Trees
works.credit: Vincent van Gogh. Olive Trees. Image credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, The William Hood Dunwoody Fund. Public Domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Proportional resize and JPEG compression; full source frame retained.
works.description: The twisted trees remain separate from the ochre ground, but the strokes running through both give them related forms of activity. Van Gogh does not reserve movement for foliage stirred by weather. Sky and earth participate too. The blue mountains steady the distance, allowing the densely worked foreground to remain legible as a rooted grove rather than an undifferentiated pattern.

works.title: Lucretia
works.credit: Rembrandt van Rijn. Lucretia. Image credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, The William Hood Dunwoody Fund. Public Domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Proportional resize and JPEG compression; full source frame retained.
works.description: The stain on the undergarment places this moment after Lucretia has wounded herself. Rembrandt gives her no triumphant gesture: the lowered gaze and hand raised towards a cord keep attention on a vulnerable body. The ancient story has often served public ideas of honour. Here its consequence is concentrated in cloth, blood and the effort required simply to remain upright.

works.title: Hortense Valpinçon
works.credit: Edgar Degas. Portrait of Mlle. Hortense Valpinçon. Image credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, The John R. Van Derlip Fund. Public Domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Proportional resize and JPEG compression; full source frame retained.
works.description: The girl's leaning pose interrupts the room's busy patterns. Degas gives her enough informality to appear occupied in her own setting, while the turned head keeps her available to the portrait. Flowers and furnishings could easily dominate such a small figure. Instead, their density makes her particular arrangement of hands, shoulders and face a clearer point of attention.

works.title: The Japanese Bridge
works.credit: Claude Monet. The Japanese Bridge. Image credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, Bequest of Putnam Dana McMillan. Public Domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Proportional resize and JPEG compression; full source frame retained.
works.description: The bridge has to be found within dense red, blue, yellow and green marks. In this late Monet, familiar architecture no longer provides a clean outline around which colour can be arranged. Recognition depends on a few surviving relations. The garden remains the subject, but the painting gives unusual weight to the point at which a known place becomes difficult to separate from paint.

works.title: The Mill Stream, Montclair, New Jersey
works.catalogueTitle: The Mill Stream, Montclair, New Jersey
works.credit: George Inness. The Mill Stream, Montclair, New Jersey. George Inness; Minneapolis Institute of Art; Gift of Don and Diana Lee Lucker. Public Domain Mark 1.0 (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Full-frame proportional resize and JPEG compression.
works.description: Roofs and chimneys remain visible beyond the thin trees, even as warm light softens their separation from the landscape. Inness does not need to remove industry to achieve continuity. The blurred reflections help join built and natural forms within the same atmosphere. Look for where an edge remains firm and where it yields: that variation carries the view's coherence.

works.title: The Death of Germanicus
works.credit: The Death of Germanicus. WikiArt; Nicolas Poussin. Proportional resizing and JPEG compression; source frame preserved.
works.description: Extended arms connect the dying man's bed with the soldiers, while the family occupies another part of the gathering. Poussin keeps different responses legible rather than making grief a single repeated expression. Deep blue drapery holds the scene together above them. Public obligation and private loss share a room, but the figures' positions prevent those experiences from becoming interchangeable.

works.title: City Night
works.credit: Georgia O'Keeffe. City Night. Image: WikiArt. Copyright protected (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: O'Keeffe leaves only a narrow interval of sky between the rising buildings. From this upward angle, the city is less a collection of addresses than a structure enclosing the observer. A small light near the lower edge sharpens the difference in scale. The broad dark masses make height palpable without requiring windows or street activity to be described individually.

works.title: Our Nurse, Margaret Burgess
works.catalogueTitle: Portrait of Our Nurse, Margaret Burgess
works.credit: Florine Stettheimer. Portrait of Our Nurse, Margaret Burgess. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Stettheimer names the household worker and gives her an elongated, central presence within a setting of small objects and figures. Scale follows the painting's decorative arrangement rather than a consistently measured room. The title's possessive phrase records a household relationship, but Margaret Burgess is not reduced to an anonymous function. Her name anchors the invented world around her.

works.title: Self-Portrait with Dr Arrieta
works.credit: Francisco Goya. Self-Portrait with Dr. Arrieta. Image credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, The Ethel Morrison Van Derlip Fund. Public Domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Proportional resize and JPEG compression; full source frame retained.
works.description: Goya represents himself unable to maintain the self-sufficient pose of a conventional portrait. Arrieta supports him and brings a glass towards his mouth. The doctor's practical action gives the image its structure: one body makes the other's position possible. The shadowy company behind them cannot compete with this specific account of care at close quarters.

works.title: Under the Pandanus
works.catalogueTitle: I Raro Te Oviri (Under the Pandanus)
works.credit: Paul Gauguin. I Raro Te Oviri (Under the Pandanus). Image credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, The William Hood Dunwoody Fund. Public Domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Proportional resize and JPEG compression; full source frame retained.
works.description: Purple ground and patterned foliage give the setting an order that does not depend on naturalistic colour. Gauguin places the women and dark animal within that constructed field. Its visual coherence should not be confused with a transparent account of Tahitian life. The painting shows, among other things, a European artist deciding how a place and its people will appear.

works.title: White Plumes
works.credit: Henri Matisse. White Plumes. Image credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, The William Hood Dunwoody Fund. Public Domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Proportional resize and JPEG compression; full source frame retained.
works.description: The feathered hat spreads well beyond the head, giving an accessory much of the portrait's pictorial weight. Matisse balances it against the red background, dark hair and pale clothing. The sitter's face must hold its place within this competition of shapes. Costume is therefore more than information about fashion; it changes the proportions through which the person is seen.

works.title: Self-Portrait with a Detachable Collar
works.credit: Frédéric Bazille. Self-Portrait with Detachable Collar. Frédéric Bazille; Minneapolis Institute of Art; The John R. Van Derlip Fund. Public Domain Mark 1.0 (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Full-frame proportional resize and JPEG compression.
works.description: A narrow white collar separates Bazille's head from the darker jacket and background. With so few bright accents available, that small piece of clothing acquires structural importance. The slightly turned face can emerge without a studio, palette or other explanatory prop. The likeness depends on measured differences of tone rather than an inventory of the painter's profession.

works.title: Self-Portrait
works.credit: Antonio Mancini. Self-Portrait. Antonio Mancini; Minneapolis Institute of Art; The Putnam Dana McMillan Fund; 71.50. Public Domain Mark 1.0 (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Full-frame proportional resize and JPEG compression.
works.description: Mancini's face emerges unevenly, broken by rough highlights and areas that remain in shadow. The paint does not offer every feature with the same clarity. Recognition persists despite these omissions, making the process of finding a face part of looking at the portrait. Compare Bazille's clean collar: two small self-images can set very different conditions for becoming visible.

works.title: Saint Anthony Falls as It Appeared in 1848
works.catalogueTitle: St. Anthony Falls as It Appeared in 1848
works.credit: Henry Lewis. St. Anthony Falls as It Appeared in 1848. Henry Lewis; Minneapolis Institute of Art; Gift of E. C. Gale; 28.79. Public Domain Mark 1.0 (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Full-frame proportional resize and JPEG compression.
works.description: The date in Lewis's title belongs to the scene represented, not to the painting's manufacture in 1855. That distinction gives this river view a retrospective character. Falls, islands, trees and low buildings record a particular state of the site. The broad arrangement remains a composed landscape, even while the title asks it to serve as a historical account.

works.title: A Pond in the Morvan
works.credit: Charles-François Daubigny. A Pond in the Morvan. Charles-François Daubigny; Minneapolis Institute of Art; Gift of Mr. M. R. Schweitzer. Public Domain Mark 1.0 (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Full-frame proportional resize and JPEG compression.
works.description: Daubigny holds water and dense trees together through closely related tones. There is no conspicuous central event to organise the view, so the differences between the dark foreground, pond and warmer light become its main divisions. The scene's stillness has been constructed, not merely found. A few broad masses give the eye enough variation to remain engaged.

works.title: A Scene on the Tohickon Creek: Autumn
works.catalogueTitle: A Scene on the Tohickon Creek: Autumn
works.credit: Thomas Moran. A Scene on the Tohickon Creek: Autumn. Thomas Moran; Minneapolis Institute of Art; The Frances E. Andrews Wilderness Fund, in memory of her mother Mary Hunt Andrews; 68.82. Public Domain Mark 1.0 (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Full-frame proportional resize and JPEG compression.
works.description: The creek opens a passage through trees that might otherwise close into a continuous wall. Moran uses small falls and lighter areas of water to carry attention towards the brighter distance. The autumn foliage supplies warmth, but the stream supplies movement through the picture. Following it reveals how a crowded landscape can be made traversable to the eye.

works.title: A Vestal Virgin Tending Fire
works.credit: François Lemoyne. A Vestal Virgin Tending Fire. François Lemoyne; Minneapolis Institute of Art; The Ethel Morrison Van Derlip Fund; 65.48. Public Domain Mark 1.0 (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Full-frame proportional resize and JPEG compression.
works.description: The flame identifies the woman's ritual responsibility and lights the figure who tends it. Lemoyne brings the action close enough for the face and hands to become its principal measures. An object can have this double function without requiring an elaborate symbolic explanation: the small fire is the reason for her presence and the means by which that presence is revealed.

works.title: Abstract Painting No. 9
works.credit: Ad Reinhardt. Abstract Painting No. 9. WikiArt source label: Ad Reinhardt Fair Use. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/ad-reinhardt/abstract-painting-no-9-1966
works.license: Ad Reinhardt Fair Use (WikiArt source label)
works.description: The nearly black rectangles do not immediately separate themselves from their dark surroundings. Reinhardt removes the strong contrast that usually makes a composition quickly readable. Looking requires time for slight differences to emerge. A screen reproduction can suppress or exaggerate those differences, so the image should not be treated as a reliable substitute for the painting's exact tonal relations.

works.title: Abundant Fruit
works.credit: Severin Roesen. Abundant Fruit. Severin Roesen; Minneapolis Institute of Art; Gift of Don and Diana Lee Lucker; 2005.96. Public Domain Mark 1.0 (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Full-frame proportional resize and JPEG compression.
works.description: Roesen assembles more fruit than a casual arrangement would require, allowing whole skins, cut interiors, leaves and tendrils to compete for notice. Darkness makes the crowded display easier to distinguish. Abundance is an ordered pictorial effect: each variety has to remain sufficiently separate for the quantity to register as variety rather than a single indistinct heap.

works.title: Ichikawa Danjūrō V in a Shibaraku Role
works.catalogueTitle: Actor Ichikawa Danjūrō V in a Shibaraku Role
works.medium: Hanging scroll (nikuhitsu), ink and colour on silk
works.credit: Katsukawa Shunshō. Actor Ichikawa Danjūrō V in a Shibaraku Role. Katsukawa Shunshō; Minneapolis Institute of Art; Bequest of Richard P. Gale; 74.1.110. Public Domain Mark 1.0 (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Full-frame proportional resize and JPEG compression.
works.description: The actor's red costume, kneeling pose and long sword carry the theatrical identity without an elaborate stage around them. Shunshō uses the empty ground to make the silhouette especially legible. This is a painted hanging scroll, not a woodblock print: its economy belongs to the handling of a single image as well as to the clarity of the role.

closingSections.title: Allow different works different speeds
paragraphs: The crowded fruit and the nearly black Reinhardt do not reward the same first glance. Let the work's contrasts determine how long it takes to distinguish its parts. This is a collection-based selection, not an account of current installation. Check the museum's live records before planning a visit around a specific object, particularly works on paper or silk.
